mit-1-2-example-composition: For \(g(t)=2t+1\) and \(f(t)=4t\), composition gives \(f(g(t))=8t+4\). The resulting slope is the product of the two slopes.
mit-1-2-example-two-speed: Starting with \(f(0)=0\), a velocity of \(2\) up to \(t=5\) gives \(f(5)=10\). A velocity of \(3\) thereafter gives \(f(t)=10+3(t-5)\), with continuity at the change.
mit-1-3-example-square: For \(f(t)=t^2\), the average velocity over an increment \(h\) is \(2t+h\). As \(h\to0\), the instantaneous velocity is \(v(t)=2t\).
mit-1-4-concept-position-on-circle: A ball moves counterclockwise around the unit circle at unit speed. With angle \(t\) measured in radians, its coordinates are \(x=\cos t\) and \(y=\sin t\).
mit-1-4-definition-radian-measure: An angle in radians equals the intercepted arc length on a unit circle. A full turn is \(2\pi\) radians, or \(360^\circ\), so the ball returns after time \(t=2\pi\).
mit-1-4-rule-velocity-on-circle: Velocity is tangent to the circle and perpendicular to its radius. At unit speed its horizontal component is \(-\sin t\), and its vertical component is \(\cos t\).
mit-1-4-concept-harmonic-motion: The vertical projection performs simple harmonic motion with height \(f(t)=\sin t\). It stops at the top and bottom and moves fastest through the center.
mit-1-4-rule-slope-of-sine: When height is \(\sin t\), vertical velocity is \(\cos t\). Similarly, the derivative of \(\cos t\) is \(-\sin t\).
mit-1-4-example-double-speed: For angular position \(2t\), the coordinates are \(x=\cos2t\) and \(y=\sin2t\). The period is \(\pi\), and velocity is \((-2\sin2t,2\cos2t)\), with speed \(2\).
mit-1-5-rule-identities: The Pythagorean identity follows from \(x^2+y^2=r^2\). Addition formulas describe sine and cosine of a sum; setting the angles equal gives the double-angle formulas.
mit-1-5-example-values-2pi-3: At angle \(\frac{2\pi}{3}=120^\circ\), a point on the unit circle has coordinates \(x=-\frac12\) and \(y=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). The tangent is negative because the horizontal and vertical coordinates have opposite signs.
mit-1-6-concept-sampling-sine: The curve \(y=\sin x\) is continuous. Sampling \(y=\sin n\) only at integer values of \(n\) produces apparent patterns through interaction with the period \(2\pi\).
mit-1-6-concept-pi-approximations: Since \(\frac{22}{7}\) is close to \(\pi\), \(\sin22\) is about \(0.01\). Similarly, \(\sin44\) is about \(0.02\). Near-multiples of \(\pi\) help explain the sampled curves.
mit-1-6-concept-aliasing-moire: Integer samples can appear to trace several slowly varying curves. Their appearance depends on the sampling scale and on how closely integer steps approximate multiples of the sine period.
mit-2-1-example-x-squared: For \(f(x)=x^2\), the difference quotient is \(2x+h\). Its limit as \(h\to0\) is \(2x\), the derivative of the parabola.
mit-2-1-example-reciprocal: For \(f(x)=\frac1x\), the difference quotient simplifies to \(-\frac1{x(x+h)}\). As \(h\to0\), it tends to \(-\frac1{x^2}\), so the graph is decreasing on either side of zero.
mit-2-2-example-polynomial: Apply the power rule separately to each term of \(f(x)=2x^3-5x^2+4x-7\). The constant contributes zero to the derivative.
mit-2-3-example-tangent-parabola: For \(f(x)=x^2\) at \(x=3\), the point is \((3,9)\) and the slope is \(f'(3)=6\). The tangent is \(y=9+6(x-3)=6x-9\).
mit-2-4-concept-small-angle-limits: The derivative formulas use \(\frac{\sin h}{h}\to1\) and \(\frac{1-\cos h}{h}\to0\) as \(h\to0\). Angles are measured in radians.
mit-2-4-example-derivative-sine: Expand \(\sin(x+h)\) using the addition formula. The quotient becomes \(\sin x\,\frac{\cos h-1}{h}+\cos x\,\frac{\sin h}{h}\), whose limit is \(\cos x\).
mit-2-5-example-product: For \(y=x^3\cos x\), the product rule gives \(y'=3x^2\cos x-x^3\sin x\).
mit-2-6-example-zero-over-zero: For \(x\ne1\), factoring gives \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1\). The limit as \(x\to1\) is therefore \(2\), despite the original indeterminate form.
mit-3-1-example-square-root: To estimate \(\sqrt{4.1}\), use the tangent at \(a=4\). The estimate is \(2+\frac14(0.1)=2.025\).
mit-3-2-example-optimization: A rectangle with fixed perimeter \(P\) has area \(A(x)=x(\frac P2-x)\). Setting the derivative to zero gives \(x=\frac P4\), so the maximizing rectangle is a square.
mit-3-3-example-acceleration: For \(f(t)=\frac12at^2\), velocity is \(at\) and acceleration is \(a\). Positive acceleration gives an upward-bending parabola.
mit-3-4-example-sketch: For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), the derivative \(3x^2-3\) vanishes at \(x=\pm1\). The second derivative \(6x\) changes sign at zero.
mit-3-5-example-parabola-slope: For \(y=x^2\), the slope \(2x\) shows how the tangent changes as the point moves away from the vertex.
mit-3-6-example-cosine-iteration: Repeated cosine iteration converges to the fixed point \(x=\cos x\), approximately \(0.739\). The magnitude of the derivative near that point is below one.
mit-3-7-example-square-root: To solve \(x^2=a\) for positive \(a\), Newton's method averages a positive estimate \(x\) with \(\frac ax\).
mit-3-8-example-lhopital: For the indeterminate limit \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}\), differentiating numerator and denominator gives \(\lim_{x\to0}\cos x=1\).
mit-4-1-example-sine-of-square: For \(y=\sin(x^2)\), multiply the outer derivative \(\cos(x^2)\) by the inner derivative \(2x\).
mit-4-1-example-power-chain: For \(y=(1+x^2)^5\), the outer derivative is \(5(1+x^2)^4\), which must be multiplied by \(2x\).
mit-4-3-definition-inverse-function: An inverse reverses a one-to-one function. Its graph reflects the original graph across \(y=x\).
mit-4-3-example-inverse-cube: The inverse of \(y=x^3\) is \(x=y^{1/3}\). Its derivative is \(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac13y^{-2/3}\) for nonzero \(y\).
mit-5-1-example-triangle-area: Under \(v=t\) from zero to \(T\), the region is a triangle with area \(\frac12T^2\). This equals the accumulated displacement.
mit-5-2-example-antiderivative: An antiderivative of \(3x^2+2\) is \(x^3+2x+C\), since its derivative returns the integrand.
mit-5-3-example-area-by-sums: Rectangular sums for \(y=x^2\) on \([0,1]\) approach \(\frac13\) as the partition is refined.
mit-5-4-example-substitution: For \(\int2x\cos(x^2)\,dx\), let \(u=x^2\) and \(du=2x\,dx\). The result is \(\sin(x^2)+C\).
mit-5-5-example-definite-integral: The area under \(y=x\) on \([0,2]\) is \(2\). Evaluating the antiderivative \(\frac{x^2}{2}\) at the endpoints gives the same result.
mit-5-6-example-average-value: The average of \(x^2\) on \([0,1]\) is the integral \(\frac13\) divided by the interval length \(1\).
mit-6-2-definition-e-and-derivative: The exponential \(e^x\) is its own derivative, making the base \(e\) especially useful in calculus.
mit-6-2-example-exp-chain: For \(y=e^{x^2}\), multiply the exponential by the derivative of the exponent to obtain \(2xe^{x^2}\).
mit-7-1-example-x-times-ex: Choose \(u=x\) and \(dv=e^x\,dx\). Integration by parts gives \(\int xe^x\,dx=xe^x-e^x+C\).
mit-8-1-example-cone-volume: Rotating \(y=\frac rhx\) over \([0,h]\) creates disks. Their accumulated volume is \(\frac13\pi r^2h\).
mit-8-2-example-arc-length: For the line \(y=2x\) on \([0,1]\), the constant slope gives arc length \(\int_0^1\sqrt{1+4}\,dx=\sqrt5\).
